extracted.intended_audience: registered patent/trademark practitioners, their counsel, and USPTO/OED staff involved in reciprocal disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements for imposing identical reciprocal discipline on USPTO practitioners based on a state's disciplinary adjudication, including the Selling v. Radford three-part test (due process, infirmity of proof, grave injustice), burdens of proof, and requirements for nunc pro tune treatment under 37 C.F.R. § 11.24 and related rules (e.g., § 11.58, § 11.59).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling / 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d) standard (three exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: State disbarment creates a federal presumption that imposition of reciprocal discipline is proper unless an independent review reveals (1) a want of due process, (2) an infirmity of proof of the misconduct, or (3) that grave injustice would result from imposing reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation mirrors Selling v. Radford: the USPTO Director shall impose identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, suspension, disbarment, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner demonstrates by clear and convincing evidence a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the enumerated exceptions. Courts and the USPTO treat these exceptions narrowly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner's burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent must demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that there is a genuine issue of material fact as to one of the § 11.24(d)(1) factors (due process deprivation, infirmity of proof, or grave injustice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a high, narrow standard: mere disagreement with the state tribunal's findings or garden-variety evidentiary complaints do not meet it. The USPTO and federal courts consistently require clear-and-convincing proof to overcome the presumption in favor of reciprocal discipline. Affirmative defenses generally carry the same clear-and-convincing burden under 37 C.F.R. § 11.49.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process deprivation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: To negate reciprocal discipline on due-process grounds, the practitioner must show that the state proceeding was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute a deprivation of due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process requires reasonable notice of the charges and an opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner (ability to present evidence, testify, call and cross-examine witnesses, and make argument). Attendance and active participation in hearings, representation by counsel, and ability to appeal generally defeat a due-process claim. Relitigating substantive rulings or contesting evidentiary decisions does not establish a due-process deprivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infirmity of proof criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish infirmity of proof, the practitioner must show such defects in the evidentiary support for the state tribunal's findings that the USPTO could not, consistent with its duty, accept the state's conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a difficult showing; deference is given to the trier of fact on credibility determinations. Mere disagreement about credibility, factual findings, or legal conclusions is insufficient. Allegations of false or unauthenticated evidence must be proved clearly and convincingly and are routinely rejected where they merely attempt to relitigate the state proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave injustice criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid reciprocal discipline on grave-injustice grounds, the practitioner must show that imposing the identical discipline would result in grave injustice — e.g., the punishment is so ill-fitted to the adjudicated misconduct that to impose it would be inequitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry is whether the sanction 'fits' the misconduct; courts consider mitigating factors and whether the state sanction was within the appropriate range. If the state penalty is within the normal range, reciprocal imposition is not a grave injustice. Economic hardship or loss of income is generally insufficient to establish grave injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nunc pro tunc (concurrent) reciprocal discipline requirements (§11.24(c) and §11.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent (nunc pro tunc) imposition of reciprocal discipline is available only if the practitioner promptly notified the OED Director of the out-of-jurisdiction discipline and establishes by clear and convincing evidence that the practitioner voluntarily ceased all activities before the USPTO and complied with the duties set forth in § 11.58.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: § 11.58 duties include filing notices of withdrawal in pending matters, notifying jurisdictions and clients, returning unearned fees and client property, complying with advertising rules, and filing required affidavits/recordkeeping. Voluntary cessation of some practice alone is insufficient; full compliance with § 11.58 and timely notice to USPTO are prerequisites. The respondent bears the burden to prove compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirements for initiating reciprocal discipline (certified order, notice, and timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director must obtain a certified copy of the record or order regarding the state discipline and provide the practitioner with a Notice and Order, including a copy of the record or order, as required by 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(a)-(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtaining a certified copy of the state order establishes a prima facie case by clear and convincing evidence of the out-of-jurisdiction discipline. The Notice and Order should be accompanied by the record or order; the rules do not require the certified copy to be attached to the practitioner's initial Notice if certification was obtained and the record/order provided as permitted by the rules. The OED Director must also timely act on grievances (the Complaint here was filed within the one-year rule referenced in the decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent's duty to notify USPTO and timing obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner disciplined in another jurisdiction is required to notify the USPTO of that discipline within 30 days (per 37 C.F.R. § 11.24(a) / related rules), and the OED Director must maintain and act on grievances in a timely manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to timely notify USPTO of out-of-jurisdiction discipline is a separate regulatory violation and precludes nunc pro tunc (concurrent) treatment. Proof that the practitioner did not notify USPTO is a ground for denying requests for concurrent application of discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of review — not a de novo proceeding; limited role of USPTO Director
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocal disciplinary proceedings are not de novo reviews of the state proceeding; the USPTO Director is not a court of review to discover errors in the state tribunal's proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director's role is to consider the record and determine whether one of the narrow § 11.24(d) exceptions applies. Broad relitigation of the state case, challenges to evidentiary rulings, or reweighing credibility are improper. The Director may, however, permit supplementation of the record where appropriate; both parties may be allowed to augment the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary discretion and supplementation of the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunals have broad discretion to admit or refuse evidence, and the USPTO Director may allow parties to supplement or augment the record in reciprocal-discipline proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing supplementation is a long-established practice and does not prejudice parties if conducted properly. However, even with supplementation, the Director gives deference to the state tribunal's factfinding and credibility determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies, orders, and administrative consequences upon reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: When reciprocal discipline is imposed, the Director may order exclusion/disbarment/suspension from practice before the USPTO and issue ancillary administrative directives (publish notice in the Official Gazette, give notice under § 11.59 to state agencies and courts, require compliance with § 11.58 duties, dissociate USPTO customer numbers, and bar reapplication until reinstated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final orders may include publication of a Notice of Exclusion describing the grounds, instruction to notify jurisdictions and clients, administrative dissociation of practitioner accounts, and prohibition on obtaining or being added to Customer Numbers until USPTO reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on respondent for affirmative defenses (§11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent asserting any affirmative defense in a USPTO disciplinary proceeding bears the burden of proving that defense by clear and convincing evidence, per 37 C.F.R. § 11.49.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aligns with the high evidentiary standard applied to the § 11.24(d) exceptions and requires robust proof for claims such as untimeliness, lack of jurisdiction, or challenges to the sufficiency of the state's discipline record.
